t: Circular Permutation in Binary Representation — Gray Code with XOR Offset
o: We need a permutation of all $2^n$ numbers starting at `start`, where consecutive elements (including the wrap-around pair) differ in exactly one bit. This is exactly the **cyclic Gray code** sequence, just rotated so it begins at `start`. In Example 1 (`n=2, start=3`), the standard Gray code is `00,01,11,10` = `[0,1,3,2]`; rotating it to start at 3 gives `[3,2,0,1]`. Since $n \le 16$, we have at most 65536 elements, so any linear-time construction is trivially fast; even backtracking would work but is unnecessary.
k: The standard binary-reflected Gray code is `g(i) = i ^ (i >> 1)`, which lists all $2^n$ values with each consecutive pair differing by one bit.
XOR-ing every element of a Gray code sequence by a constant `start` preserves the one-bit-difference property and rotates the sequence to begin at `start`.
The Gray code is cyclic: `g(0)=0` and `g(2^n - 1)` differ only in the top bit, and XOR is preserved under the constant offset.

a.i: Try to build the permutation element by element: from the current number, try flipping each bit to get an unused neighbor. If we reach a dead end, backtrack. With $2^{16}$ states this is exponential in the worst case but works for small n; it directly mirrors the problem statement without needing any math insight.
s: Start the path with `start` and mark it visited.
At each step, try every bit flip `cur ^ (1 << b)` that is unvisited.
Recurse; if the path reaches length $2^n$ and the last element differs from `start` by one bit, return the path.
Otherwise undo the choice and try the next bit.
a.t: Exponential worst case $O(2^n \cdot n)$ due to backtracking, though in practice it finds a path quickly.
a.sp: $O(2^n)$ for the visited array, result list, and recursion stack.

a.n: Approach 2: Gray code with XOR offset (optimal)
a.i: The binary-reflected Gray code `g(i) = i ^ (i >> 1)` visits every number in $[0, 2^n)$ exactly once, consecutive entries differ in exactly one bit, and it is cyclic since `g(0)=0` and `g(2^n-1)` differ only in the top bit. XOR-ing every element with a fixed constant `start` is a bijection on the hypercube that maps edges to edges, so the resulting sequence still has all required properties, and its first element is `g(0) ^ start = start`.
s: For each index `i` from 0 to $2^n - 1$, compute the Gray code value `g = i ^ (i >> 1)`.
Output `g ^ start` as the i-th element.
a.sp: $O(1)$ extra space beyond the output array.

w: In an interview, mention the brute force briefly to show you understand the structure, then present the Gray-code solution as the optimal answer — it is a one-liner per element and clearly correct. Common pitfalls: forgetting the cyclic condition (the last element must also differ from the first by one bit — the Gray code guarantees this automatically), off-by-one errors in the loop bound ($2^n$, not $2^n - 1$), and assuming rotation alone suffices (rotating a Gray code does keep adjacency, but the simple XOR trick is cleaner and starts exactly at `start`). Edge cases: `n = 1` gives two elements like `[start, start ^ 1]`; `start = 0` yields the plain Gray code. Likely follow-ups: prove why `i ^ (i >> 1)` yields adjacent codes differing in one bit (only the lowest set bit of `i` changes when incrementing), or generate the sequence iteratively via reflection instead of the formula.
